docs.title: ETECSA RF Lab
docs.text:
Research baseline No approved antenna blueprint yet No active cellular repeater designs

ETECSA RF Lab is a practical engineering project for low-cost, blackout-resilient communication on ETECSA/Cubacel service in Cuba, especially for a target installation in Matanzas.

The project focuses on ordinary phones, passive antennas, passive phone couplers, safe field testing, and data transport by USB, Ethernet, or Wi-Fi after cellular reception.

docs.title: What This Project Is
docs.text:
This project is a public engineering notebook and manual for:

  • documenting the communication problem during long blackouts
  • testing which ETECSA bands and locations actually work
  • comparing passive antenna and coupler ideas
  • building standard operating procedures for safe field work
  • creating public blueprints only after calculation, simulation, and review
  • helping collaborators continue without relying on chat memory

docs.title: What This Project Is Not
docs.text:
This project does not design or recommend:

  • active cellular RF repeaters
  • cellular power amplifiers
  • jammers
  • IMSI catchers
  • base station emulators
  • unauthorized transmitters
  • systems intended to bypass ETECSA controls

docs.title: Track A: Phone First
docs.text:
Put an ordinary ETECSA-compatible phone where the signal is best, then move data into the house.

ETECSA network
-> phone at best RF location
-> USB, Wi-Fi, or Ethernet
-> router or access point
-> house Wi-Fi

docs.title: Track B: Improved Passive System
docs.text:
Study and improve a local passive concept:

directional antenna
-> coax
-> passive phone coupler
-> ordinary phone

This track is useful only if measurement proves the passive coupler and antenna system gives repeatable benefit.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: Status: CONCEPT

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Bring usable ETECSA/Cubacel connectivity into the house during blackouts while avoiding unauthorized active cellular RF systems.

docs.title: Preferred Architecture
docs.text:
ETECSA surviving tower
-> best available RF location
-> ordinary phone with ETECSA SIM
-> USB tethering, Wi-Fi hotspot, or Ethernet adapter
-> router, access point, bridge, or travel router
-> house Wi-Fi

docs.title: Architecture Principles
docs.text:
• Put the cellular device where the signal is best.
  • Convert cellular RF to data as early as practical.
  • Transport data instead of weak RF when possible.
  • Keep the system modular and repairable.
  • Prefer parts that can be replaced independently.
  • Avoid designs that require specialized carrier service unless all low-cost paths fail.

docs.title: Passive RF Alternative
docs.text:
The passive antenna and phone-coupler track may be useful when the phone cannot be placed at the best RF location or when a local-style passive kit can be improved.

This alternative is still research-stage and requires measured coupler performance.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
No approved blueprints yet

The project is intentionally not jumping straight to final fabrication dimensions. Blueprints move through documented status levels.

docs.title: Status Levels
docs.text: Status Meaning CONCEPT Idea or topology under discussion. CALCULATED Key dimensions and assumptions calculated. SIMULATED Modeled with documented tool, geometry, and assumptions. PROTOTYPE Built or ready for prototype construction. FIELD_TESTED Tested in real conditions with stored measurements. APPROVED Reviewed design with required evidence and limitations.

docs.title: Current Blueprint State
docs.text:
Area Current Status Public Note Broadband LPDA CONCEPT Preliminary numbers are not approved build data. 1800 MHz Yagi CONCEPT Depends on LTE Band 3 availability during useful outage windows. 900 MHz Yagi CONCEPT Depends on local low-band blackout measurements. Passive phone coupler CONCEPT Needs fixture design and repeatable position sweeps.

For plain-language build paths, use Keep It Simple. That section avoids RF math and shows only the simple blueprint, materials, and build/test steps for each project path.

docs.title: Public Blueprint Rule
docs.text:
Every public blueprint must include:

  • title
  • version
  • status
  • author or AI
  • date
  • assumptions
  • target bands
  • materials
  • dimensions
  • RF calculations
  • simulation method and results
  • expected impedance or matching behavior
  • mechanical notes
  • construction tolerance
  • weatherproofing
  • limitations
  • testing procedure
  • revision history

If it has not been field tested, it must say:

NOT FIELD VALIDATED

docs.title: Website Contribution Rules
docs.text:
The public website source lives in docs/ and is built with MkDocs.

If you edit website source files or mkdocs.yml:

  1. Run mkdocs build --strict.
  2. Copy the generated output to the repository root with cp -R site/. ..
  3. Commit both the source files and generated root output.

GitHub Pages currently serves the repository root from main. Do not assume the ignored site/ folder is published.

docs.title: Keep It Simple Rules
docs.text:
The Keep It Simple section is for public, plain-language instructions. Keep it bilingual and focused on:

  • simple blueprints
  • materials
  • building instructions
  • simple test steps
  • clear status labels

Do not add RF math, unresolved engineering debate, or unapproved final dimensions there.

docs.title: Good First Contributions
docs.text:
• Add official or reputable sources for current ETECSA band information.
  • Add exact Cuban import rule citations.
  • Add first field measurements from the target locations.
  • Identify the available Android phone model and supported bands.
  • Add manufacturer attenuation data for realistic coax options.

docs.title: Data Templates
docs.text:
Measurement template ready

The project needs real measurements more than guesses. Store raw measurements in data/raw/ and keep processed summaries in data/processed/.

docs.title: Blackout Measurement Template
docs.text:
Use this CSV template:

data/templates/blackout_measurement.csv

Required columns:

date,time,location,phone_model,network_type,band,earfcn,rsrp_dbm,rsrq_db,sinr_db,rssi_dbm,ping_ms,download_mbps,upload_mbps,whatsapp_text,whatsapp_call,imo_call,antenna_type,antenna_azimuth,antenna_height_m,blackout_duration,notes

docs.title: Measurement Priorities
docs.text:
1. Indoor baseline.
  2. High window.
  3. Outside wall.
  4. Roof or highest safe point.
  5. Street corner.
  6. Same locations during blackout.

docs.title: Reporting Quality
docs.text:
• Keep raw readings.
  • Record phone model.
  • Record whether the phone is handheld, fixed, in a case, or near a coupler.
  • Record app-level success, not just signal strength.
  • Do not optimize only for strongest RSRP if SINR becomes worse.

docs.title: RF Terms
docs.text:
RSRP: Reference Signal Received Power. LTE signal power indicator, usually in dBm.

RSRQ: Reference Signal Received Quality. LTE quality indicator in dB.

SINR: Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio. Higher is generally better.

RSSI: Received Signal Strength Indicator. Broad received power indicator.

VSWR: Voltage Standing Wave Ratio. Indicates impedance mismatch.

Return loss: A measure of reflected power caused by mismatch.

EARFCN: LTE channel number.

Band 3: LTE band around 1800 MHz.

Band 8: UMTS/LTE band around 900 MHz, depending on technology and deployment.

LPDA: Log-periodic dipole array, a broadband directional antenna topology.

Yagi-Uda: Directional antenna using driven, reflector, and director elements.

docs.title: Project Terms
docs.text:
Passive coupler: A non-amplified structure that couples energy between coax or an antenna element and a phone internal antenna.

Routerless architecture: A design using an ordinary phone as the cellular modem rather than a dedicated LTE router.

Blueprint status: One of CONCEPT, CALCULATED, SIMULATED, PROTOTYPE, FIELD_TESTED, or APPROVED.

docs.title: Project Methodology
docs.text: Status: active roadmap

docs.title: Phase 0: Repository and Research Baseline
docs.text:
• Create repository structure.
  • Record known facts, assumptions, questions, and safety limits.
  • Gather dated ETECSA band and blackout behavior sources.

docs.title: Phase 1: Verify ETECSA RF Environment
docs.text:
• Measure indoor, outdoor, window, roof, and street-corner signal.
  • Record network type, band, RSRP, RSRQ, SINR, ping, upload, download, and app success.
  • Repeat during normal power and blackout.

docs.title: Phase 2: Model Antennas
docs.text:
• Compare LPDA, 900 MHz Yagi, 1800 MHz Yagi, biquad, panel, reflector, and dual-polarized options.
  • Account for material diameter, spacing, feed impedance, supports, and coax loss.

docs.title: Phase 3: Design Passive Phone Coupler
docs.text:
• Build an adjustable test fixture.
  • Sweep phone position, gap, rotation, and coupler geometry.
  • Record repeatability and sensitivity.

docs.title: Phase 4: Build Prototypes
docs.text:
• Build only designs that have calculations and simulation notes.
  • Document tolerances, materials, and assembly steps.

docs.title: Phase 5: NanoVNA Validation
docs.text:
• Calibrate NanoVNA.
  • Measure S11, return loss, SWR, resonance, and bandwidth.
  • Do not claim antenna gain from NanoVNA data alone.

docs.title: Phase 6: Blackout Field Testing
docs.text:
• Test real communication performance during outages.
  • Record app-level success, not just signal strength.

docs.title: Phase 7: Optimize
docs.text:
• Compare measured results to simulation.
  • Revise antenna, coupler, feedline, and placement.

docs.title: Phase 8: Create Final Blueprints
docs.text:
• Move only reviewed, calculated, simulated, and tested designs toward approval.
  • Clearly label anything that is not field validated.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: Status: baseline safety notes

docs.title: RF and Legal Safety
docs.text: This project is receive-focused and must use ordinary phones operating normally on the ETECSA/Cubacel network. Do not design or build unauthorized active cellular repeaters, amplifiers, transmitters, base stations, or interference devices.

docs.title: Roof and Mast Work
docs.text:
• Do not work on roofs during rain, wind, lightning, or poor visibility.
  • Keep antennas, masts, ladders, and tools away from power lines.
  • Use fall protection when appropriate.
  • Do not install anything that can fall into public space or damage nearby property.

docs.title: Lightning and Grounding
docs.text:
• Outdoor metal antennas and masts can attract or conduct lightning energy.
  • Document grounding, bonding, and surge protection before outdoor installation.
  • Disconnect test equipment during storms.
  • Do not route coax or cables in ways that create fire or shock hazards.

docs.title: Water Ingress
docs.text:
• Weatherproof outdoor enclosures and coax connectors.
  • Use drip loops.
  • Avoid trapping condensation around phones, batteries, or USB adapters.

docs.title: Solar DC and Batteries
docs.text:
• Fuse battery circuits appropriately.
  • Avoid undersized wires.
  • Keep batteries ventilated where required.
  • Protect USB adapters and routers from overheating.

docs.title: Field Testing
docs.text:
• Do not climb or adjust antennas alone.
  • Log test conditions so results can be repeated.
  • Stop testing if the installation becomes unsafe.

docs.title: Materials / Materiales
docs.text:
EnglishEspañol

Use simple, replaceable parts:

  • ordinary Android phone that works with ETECSA/Cubacel
  • ETECSA SIM
  • phone charger
  • USB cable

docs.title: Build Steps / Pasos De Construcción
docs.text:
EnglishEspañol
  1. Find the best safe signal place with the phone.
  2. Test these places: inside, high window, outside wall, roof edge, and street corner.
  3. Put the phone in the best safe place.
  4. Turn on USB tethering or Wi-Fi hotspot.
  5. Connect the phone to the router or access point.
  6. Connect the house devices to the router Wi-Fi.
  7. Test WhatsApp text, WhatsApp call, IMO call, and basic Internet.
  8. Write down the signal and what worked.
  1. Busca el mejor lugar seguro con señal usando el teléfono.
  2. Prueba estos lugares: dentro de la casa, ventana alta, pared exterior, borde del techo y esquina de la calle.
  3. Pon el teléfono en el mejor lugar seguro.
  4. Activa USB tethering o el punto Wi-Fi del teléfono.
  5. Conecta el teléfono al router o punto de acceso.
  6. Conecta los equipos de la casa al Wi-Fi del router.
  7. Prueba texto por WhatsApp, llamada por WhatsApp, llamada por IMO e Internet básico.
  8. Anota la señal y lo que funcionó.

docs.title: Building Instructions / Instrucciones De Construcción
docs.text:
EnglishEspañol

Use these steps only for experiments until a real blueprint is approved:

  1. Choose a safe outdoor place with better signal.
  2. Keep the coax cable as short as possible.
  3. Put the phone coupler close to the phone, but do not glue it permanently.
  4. Make the phone holder adjustable.
  5. Test different phone positions.
  6. Test different phone distances from the coupler.
  7. Point the antenna slowly in different directions.
  8. Record the best direction and phone position.
  9. Compare with the phone alone in the same place.

Usa estos pasos solo para experimentos hasta que exista un plano real aprobado:

  1. Escoge un lugar exterior seguro con mejor señal.
  2. Mantén el cable coaxial lo más corto posible.
  3. Pon el acoplador cerca del teléfono, pero no lo pegues de forma permanente.
  4. Haz que el soporte del teléfono sea ajustable.
  5. Prueba varias posiciones del teléfono.
  6. Prueba varias distancias entre el teléfono y el acoplador.
  7. Gira la antena lentamente en diferentes direcciones.
  8. Anota la mejor dirección y posición del teléfono.
  9. Compara con el teléfono solo en el mismo lugar.

The repository is currently using branch-based GitHub Pages from main.

To make that deployment match the local MkDocs preview, the generated MkDocs static output is committed at the repository root:

assets/
search/
architecture/
sops/

The .nojekyll file tells GitHub Pages to serve these files as plain static output.

The workflow at .github/workflows/pages.yml validates the MkDocs build on pushes to main, but it does not deploy.

For the current branch-based setup:

  3. Under Build and deployment, use Deploy from a branch.
  4. Select branch main.
  5. Select folder /root.
  6. Save.

For a public project site, the repository should be public or otherwise on a GitHub plan that allows Pages for the repository visibility.

These SOPs are intended to keep measurements repeatable and safe. They are not a substitute for local safety judgment.

docs.title: Minimum Field Safety Rules
docs.text:
• Do not climb or work near outdoor wiring during unsafe weather.
  • Keep masts, antennas, ladders, and tools away from power lines.
  • Do not test on roofs alone.
  • Do not handle outdoor antenna systems during lightning risk.
  • Stop the test if the setup becomes unsafe.

docs.title: Blackout Measurement Sequence
docs.text:
1. Power the existing Nauta Hogar modem/router from solar if possible.
  2. Check DSL synchronization.
  3. Test Internet over DSL.
  4. Measure phone service indoors.
  5. Measure service at high window, outside wall, roof or highest safe point, and street corner.
  6. Record network type, band, RSRP, RSRQ, SINR, ping, upload, download, and app success.
  7. Record blackout duration and notes.

docs.title: RF Reporting Rule
docs.text: Phone signal improvement is a system result. Do not call it antenna gain unless gain was measured with a method appropriate for antenna gain.
